extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; educated public, naturalists and amateur scientists
extracted.subtask_short: classifying fossil as bird or reptile
extracted.subtask_description: Use osteological, integumentary, and functional-anatomy features of fossil remains (vertebrae shape, limb bones, teeth, feathers/impressions, pneumatic bones, brain casts, etc.) to determine whether a specimen should be regarded as avian, reptilian, or intermediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertebrae centra shape (bi-concave / double cup-shaped)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of bi-concave (double cup-shaped) vertebral centra in neck, back, or tail segments is characteristic of reptiles and never occurs among modern birds (except rare posterior concavity in a few birds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper repeatedly notes bi-concave vertebrae as a 'strongly non-Avian description' (e.g., 'the neck, back, and tail vertebrae preserved, all show this character...resembling those in the plesiosaurs'). Use this as a key reptilian indicator, though consider other bones before concluding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breastbone shape and keel presence
rubrics_metrics.description: A prominently keeled breastbone is typical of flying birds; a thin, weak breastbone without a keel (as in ostrich or apteryx) suggests flightlessness or divergence from volant birds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ichthyornis shows a 'prominently keeled breastbone' typical of birds; Hesperornis has a 'breastbone... thin and weak, and entirely without a keel.' Presence/absence and form of the keel inform flight capability and avian affinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Furcula (collar-bone) morphology
rubrics_metrics.description: Union of the collar-bones to form a 'merry-thought' (furcula) is a typical avian feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites 'the collar-bone united to form a "merry-thought,"' among marks typical of the bird tribe. Use as positive evidence for avian classification when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wing and limb proportions / wing bone structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative proportions of wing to hind limbs and the size/structure of wing bones indicate volant vs non-volant habits and avian affinity (e.g., large wings relative to hind limbs, elongated wing bones indicate flying birds; rudimentary/diminutive wings indicate flightlessness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ichthyornis had 'wings large in proportion to the posterior extremities'; Hesperornis had 'wing-bones are diminutive, and the wings are rudimentary and useless as organs of flight.' Also consider presence/absence of free digits (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tooth presence, implantation (sockets vs groove), and morphology
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether teeth are present, how they are implanted (distinct sockets vs set in a groove), and their shape (compressed, acute summits, enamel-covered crowns) are diagnostic: teeth in sockets and reptilian-style crowns suggest reptilian affinities; birds are typically toothless or have different jaw denticulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ichthyornis teeth 'implanted in distinct sockets'; Hesperornis teeth 'not in sockets but set in a groove.' Tooth form (e.g., 'compressed, with very acute summits', 'crowns covered with enamel and supported on stout fangs') and similarity to Mososauroids or Maestricht reptiles used as comparative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tooth replacement method
rubrics_metrics.description: Mode of tooth replacement — e.g., successors implanted in cavities in fangs, hollow cone filled with pulp producing replacement from within — is characteristic of some reptiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes some preserved teeth 'have the crowns of their successors implanted in cavities in their fangs,' and describes the reptilian replacement process. Use replacement pattern as evidence toward reptilian identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail vertebrae number, articulation and specializations
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of caudal segments, degree of fusion, and processes on tail vertebrae (e.g., long flattened processes preventing lateral motion, fused terminal mass) are diagnostic of locomotory function and avian vs reptilian character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hesperornis tail had 'no fewer than twelve segments' with 'very long and horizontally flattened processes which prevent all motion in a lateral direction' suggesting vertical movement (diving aid). Archaeopteryx had twenty caudal segments each supporting quill-feathers. Tail architecture may indicate swimming adaptation or feathered tail in birds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand/wing digits (fused vs free) and presence of claws
rubrics_metrics.description: In modern birds the fingers are fused into one mass; free digits with claws on the manual region (as in Archaeopteryx) are reptilian-like features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper highlights Archaeopteryx where 'the fingers... are not bound together — they are free' and several ended in 'a strong-curved claw.' Use free, clawed digits as evidence of intermediate/reptilian characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feathers or integumentary impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct preservation of feathers or plumage impressions (down, quill feathers) is strong evidence of avian affinity and of warm-bloodedness / insulating covering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solenhofen slabs preserve 'casts of the down and feathers' and impressions; the presence of feathers is contrasted with bony scales/hardened coverings in reptiles. Absence of feather impressions in well-preserving deposits (where feathers would be preserved) is used as evidence for reptilian (cold-blooded) interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pneumaticity / air-passages in bones and inferred respiratory system
rubrics_metrics.description: Air-passages in skull, spine, and limb bones (pneumatic bones) that coincide with those in birds indicate a bird-like air circulation system and support warm-bloodedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prof. Seeley argued that air-passages 'coincide identically in situation with those in birds' and from this inferred 'a system of air-circulation from the lungs similar to what is found in birds' and possibly warm-bloodedness. Use pneumaticity as evidence favoring avian affinities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brain morphology (casts / lobes arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form and arrangement of brain lobes (from natural endocasts) comparable to modern bird brains indicate avian affinities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeley's casts of skull interiors led him to claim 'the resemblance of form and arrangement of parts between this fossil animal's brain and the brain of a bird amounts... to absolute identity.' Use endocast morphology as a high-value character where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Haunch/hip-girdle conformation and union to spine
rubrics_metrics.description: Form of the haunch-bone (pelvis), whether portions remain as separate bones, and whether the pelvis is firmly joined to the spine by bony union are informative: reptilian-like permanence of separate pelvic bones and lack of firm bony union to spine may indicate reptilian affinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes the haunch-bone 'presents some resemblance to... reptiles, in the permanence as separate bones... and in its not being firmly joined to the spine by bony union as in ordinary birds.' Use pelvic structure to weigh reptilian vs avian assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hock / tarsal bone fusion pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a single coalesced hock bone (as in birds) versus three distinct, immovably fitting bones (as in some reptiles) is diagnostic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compsognathus lacks the 'merry-thought' and 'the single hock-bone of the bird replaced by three distinct bones, fitting immovably together.' Consider tarsal fusion as a character for locomotor mode and clade affinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body covering inference and metabolic implications (feathers vs bony scales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of an insulating, non-conducting covering (feathers) is a constant correlative of warm-bloodedness; lack of feathers but hard bony scales suggests cold-bloodedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen argues that flying dragons lack feather impressions (despite preservation conditions that would retain feathers) and thus were 'cold-blooded'; Huxley counters that pneumatic bones indicate warm-bloodedness. Use integumentary evidence and its preservational context when inferring metabolic physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional adaptations inferred from bone articulations (e.g., swimming specializations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulation details (interlocking bones preventing flexion in certain directions, incurved lower ends of leg-bones, dorsal flattening of tail processes) indicate functional specializations (swimming, diving, bipedal hopping) that inform ecological and taxonomic interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: limb bones 'peculiarly articulated to produce rigidity and prevent flexion... increase the strength of the joints during the act of swimming'; tail processes suggesting vertical movement as a diving aid; incurved leg-bone ends as in swimming-birds. Use functional inference to support identification (e.g., aquatic bird vs reptile with convergent swimming adaptations).
